Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Former Philippine President Corazon Aquino, whose "People Power" movement pushed out longtime strongman Ferdinand Marcos less than three years after her husband's assassination, has died at age 76, her family announced Saturday. "She was the agent of change in Philippine democracy," said Ray Donato, the nation's consul-general in Atlanta. Aquino, the first woman to lead the Philippines, had been battling colon cancer since March 2008 and died of cardio-respiratory arrest at 3:18 a.m. Saturday (3:18 p.m. Friday ET), said Mai Mislang, a spokeswoman for her son, Philippine Sen. Benigno Aquino III. Funeral arrangements were being set up, Mislang said.  Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo has also announced a 10-day mourning period for the former president, said Ray Donato, the country's consul-general in Atlanta. "She was the agent of change in Philippine democracy, and almost all the Filipinos I know revered her during her presidency," Donato said. Aquino had been born into a wealthy family and was educated in the United States. She had not been involved in politics before her husband, opposition leader Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr., was gunned down at Manila's airport in August 1983 as he returned from exile. The political novice took over the leadership of her husband's movement after his death and challenged Marcos in a 1986 election, making a yellow dress her trademark and bolstered by the support of the country's Roman Catholic churches. Marcos had been backed by the United States, the former colonial power in the Philippines, for two decades as a stalwart anti-communist. He and his wife Imelda were friends of then-President Ronald Reagan and his wife, Nancy. But widespread allegations of electoral fraud and a mutiny by the country's military led the Reagan administration to withdraw its support, and Marcos went into exile in Hawaii. Aquino took office in a country with a $28 billion debt, widespread poverty and a persistent Marxist insurgency. She put in place a U.S.-style constitution that limited presidents to a single six-year term and survived seven coup attempts -- including one that was supressed with American help. She also oversaw the closure of the major U.S. military bases in the country before leaving office in 1992. The bases had been a bulwark of American power in the Pacific since the early 1900s and employed nearly 80,000 Filipinos, but Aquino's opponents argued the country was too dependent on the United States. Aquino announced in 1990 that it was time to begin negotiating the "orderly withdrawal" of U.S. forces.

(CNN) — Corazon Aquino, the former Philippine president whose “People Power” campaign removed longtime authoritarian leader Ferdinand Marcos from office less than three years after her husband was assassinated, died at 76, her family said Saturday.

Ray Donato, the Philippine consul-general in Atlanta, described Aquino as “the agent of change in Philippine democracy.”

Aquino, the first female president of the Philippines, had been fighting colon cancer since March 2008. She died from cardio-respiratory arrest at 3:18 a.m. Saturday in the Philippines—3:18 p.m. Friday ET—according to Mai Mislang, spokeswoman for Aquino’s son, Philippine Sen. Benigno Aquino III. Mislang said funeral plans were being arranged.

Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo declared a 10-day period of national mourning, Donato said. He added that nearly every Filipino he knew had deeply respected Aquino while she was president.

Born into an affluent family and educated in the United States, Aquino had no political background before the killing of her husband, opposition figure Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. He was shot at Manila’s airport in August 1983 while returning from exile.

After his death, the politically inexperienced Aquino assumed leadership of his movement. She ran against Marcos in the 1986 election, adopting a yellow dress as her signature image and drawing strong support from the Philippines’ Roman Catholic churches.

For 20 years, Marcos had received backing from the United States, the Philippines’ former colonial ruler, because he was regarded as a dependable anti-communist. Marcos and his wife, Imelda, were also friends with then-U.S. President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan.

However, extensive accusations of election fraud, along with a rebellion within the Philippine military, prompted the Reagan administration to end its support. Marcos subsequently fled into exile in Hawaii.

When Aquino became president, she inherited a nation burdened by $28 billion in debt, pervasive poverty and an ongoing Marxist insurgency. Her government established a constitution modeled on the U.S. system that restricted presidents to one six-year term. She also endured seven attempted coups, one of which was defeated with assistance from the United States.

Before stepping down in 1992, Aquino supervised the shutdown of the principal U.S. military bases in the Philippines. Those installations had served as a foundation of American influence in the Pacific since the early 20th century and provided jobs for almost 80,000 Filipinos. Aquino’s critics, however, maintained that the country relied too heavily on the United States.

In 1990, Aquino said the moment had come to negotiate an “orderly withdrawal” of American forces.

Former Philippine President Corazon “Cory” Aquino, the democracy icon who led the 1986 uprising that ended Ferdinand Marcos’s long authoritarian rule, died on August 1, 2009, after battling colon cancer. She was 76. Her death prompted an outpouring of grief across the Philippines and renewed reflection on her extraordinary transformation from a self-described housewife and political novice into the country’s first female president.

Aquino was born into a wealthy and politically prominent family, but for much of her early life she remained outside the public spotlight. She married Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., one of Marcos’s most prominent political opponents, and devoted herself largely to raising their five children while supporting her husband’s career. That changed after Ninoy Aquino was assassinated in 1983 upon returning to the Philippines from exile in the United States.

His killing galvanized public opposition to Marcos and pushed Corazon Aquino into national politics. Though she had little experience in government, she became a unifying figure for Filipinos who wanted an end to corruption, repression, and one-man rule. Her quiet manner, personal integrity, and status as Ninoy Aquino’s widow gave moral force to a movement that included religious leaders, civil society groups, business figures, and ordinary citizens.

In 1986, Aquino challenged Marcos in a presidential election marked by allegations of widespread fraud and intimidation. After the government declared Marcos the winner, opposition leaders rejected the result. The dispute helped trigger the largely peaceful “People Power” revolt, during which millions of Filipinos gathered along Manila’s Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, commonly known as EDSA. Civilians faced down troops with prayers, flowers, and appeals for peace, while senior military officials withdrew their support from Marcos.

The uprising forced Marcos and his family to leave the Philippines, bringing his roughly two decades in power to an end. Aquino assumed the presidency and became both the first woman to lead the country and a global symbol of nonviolent democratic change.

Her administration faced enormous challenges. She inherited weakened institutions, a troubled economy, political unrest, communist and separatist insurgencies, and a military divided by repeated coup attempts. Aquino moved quickly to dismantle the structures of dictatorship, restore civil liberties, free political prisoners, and reestablish democratic institutions. A new constitution, approved in 1987, limited presidential power, restored Congress, and strengthened protections for civil rights.

Aquino’s presidency was not without criticism. Her government struggled to reduce poverty, carry out land reform, and overcome the influence of entrenched political and economic elites. Supporters nevertheless credited her with steering the country through a fragile transition and, crucially, stepping down peacefully when her term ended in 1992. That transfer of power reinforced the democratic system she had helped restore.

Even after leaving office, Aquino remained an influential moral voice in Philippine public life. She spoke out when she believed democratic institutions were under threat and continued to command deep respect among many Filipinos.

Aquino was diagnosed with colon cancer in 2008. After months of treatment, her family announced that she had died in a Manila hospital. The government declared a 10-day period of national mourning, flags were lowered, and crowds gathered to pay tribute. Her funeral procession drew vast numbers of mourners, recalling the public grief that had followed her husband’s assassination more than a quarter-century earlier.

To admirers, Aquino’s legacy rested less on political skill than on courage, integrity, and her willingness to accept power without clinging to it. Her life became inseparable from the story of the Philippines’ return to democracy: a reluctant leader in yellow who helped inspire millions of people to confront dictatorship without violence.

**MANILA, Philippines** — Corazon Aquino, the former Philippine president whose rise to power through the 1986 “People Power” movement became a symbol of peaceful democratic change, died Saturday after a battle with colon cancer, her family said. She was 76.

Aquino, widely known as “Cory,” led the Philippines from 1986 to 1992 after millions of Filipinos took to the streets to oppose President Ferdinand Marcos, ending his two decades of authoritarian rule.

A self-described housewife with little political experience, Aquino entered public life after her husband, opposition leader Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., was assassinated upon returning from exile in 1983. His death intensified public anger toward the Marcos government and transformed his widow into the most prominent figure in the democratic opposition.

In the disputed 1986 presidential election, Aquino challenged Marcos amid widespread allegations of fraud. The ensuing protests drew huge crowds to Manila’s Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, where civilians confronted tanks with prayers, flowers and songs. The largely nonviolent uprising forced Marcos into exile and brought Aquino to the presidency.

As the country’s first female president, Aquino restored democratic institutions, introduced a new constitution and reopened political space after years of martial law. Her administration also faced repeated coup attempts, economic hardship, persistent inequality and criticism over the slow pace of land reform.

Aquino stepped down peacefully in 1992, establishing an important precedent for constitutional transfers of power. Though she largely withdrew from daily politics, she continued to speak out on national issues and remained an influential moral voice in the Philippines.

Supporters remembered her as an icon of courage and democracy; critics said her government failed to fully dismantle the entrenched political and economic interests that had long shaped the country. Her yellow clothing and signature “Laban” hand gesture nevertheless remained enduring symbols of resistance to dictatorship.

Aquino’s family announced in 2008 that she had been diagnosed with colon cancer. Her death prompted an outpouring of grief across the Philippines, where churches held vigils and supporters displayed yellow ribbons in her honor.

Born in 1933 into a prominent political family, Aquino entered public life reluctantly. **Corazon Aquino, Philippine President and Democratic Icon, Dies at 76**

Corazon “Cory” Aquino, the self-described housewife who helped topple a dictatorship and became the first woman president of the Philippines, died on Aug. 1, 2009, after a battle with colon cancer. She was 76.

Mrs. Aquino entered national politics with little experience and none of the commanding style associated with the country’s traditional political leaders. Yet her quiet resolve, religious faith and status as the widow of assassinated opposition leader Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. transformed her into the unifying figure of a democratic uprising.

Born Maria Corazon Cojuangco on Jan. 25, 1933, into a wealthy landowning family, she was educated in the Philippines and the United States. For much of her marriage, she remained outside the political spotlight while her husband became one of the most prominent critics of President Ferdinand Marcos.

Ninoy Aquino was imprisoned after Marcos imposed martial law in 1972 and later went into exile in the United States. When he returned to Manila on Aug. 21, 1983, he was shot dead as he stepped onto the airport tarmac. His assassination galvanized opposition to Marcos and thrust his widow into public life.

Initially reluctant, Mrs. Aquino emerged as the opposition’s presidential candidate when Marcos called a snap election in February 1986. Official results declared Marcos the winner, but independent observers reported extensive fraud, intimidation and vote manipulation. The disputed count triggered mass protests and defections from the military.

During four extraordinary days, millions of Filipinos gathered along Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, or EDSA, in Manila. Civilians carrying rosaries, flowers and food faced down soldiers and tanks. The largely peaceful “People Power” revolt forced Marcos into exile and brought Mrs. Aquino to the presidency on Feb. 25, 1986.

Her rise made her an international symbol of nonviolent resistance and democratic restoration. Her administration freed political prisoners, reopened democratic institutions and replaced the Marcos-era constitution with a new charter limiting presidential power. In 1987, Filipinos approved the constitution in a national referendum.

But governing proved more difficult than leading a revolution. Mrs. Aquino inherited a deeply indebted economy, a communist insurgency, regional unrest and armed forces divided by factional loyalties. Her government was also criticized for failing to deliver sweeping land reform and for relying on members of the country’s established political elite.

She survived repeated attempts by military rebels to overthrow her—commonly counted as at least six serious coup plots or attempts, along with other mutinies and destabilization efforts. The gravest came in December 1989, when rebel soldiers seized military bases and parts of Manila, and aircraft attacked the presidential palace. Loyalist forces, assisted by American fighter jets that provided air cover, eventually defeated the uprising.

The coups exposed the fragility of the restored democracy, but Mrs. Aquino’s survival became part of her legacy. She refused to abandon constitutional government or extend her time in office. In 1992, she peacefully transferred power to her elected successor, Fidel V. Ramos—an important demonstration that the presidency would once again be constrained by law.

After leaving office, Mrs. Aquino remained an influential moral voice, periodically joining protests when she believed democratic institutions were threatened. Although her presidency was marked by compromise and unfinished reforms, her place in Philippine history rested on a singular transformation: from politically inexperienced widow to the public face of a movement that ended two decades of Marcos rule.

Dressed in her signature yellow, she came to embody both the hopes and limitations of the People Power era. To supporters, her greatest achievement was not that she governed without failure, but that she restored the possibility of governing by consent.

She was survived by five children, including Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III, who was elected president the following year.
